title: The Towpath at Brougham Bridge: Hamilton, the Characteristic Function, and the Quaternions
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Dominick Street and the Uncle at Trim

stops.name: Dominick Street, Dublin: born at midnight
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The birth fell at midnight between 3 and 4 August 1805, so both dates stand in the sources; Hamilton himself later settled on the fourth, for a reason that belongs to 1835. The house is 29 Dominick Street Lower, given as 36 after a renumbering.
stops.campa: A son is born at midnight in the house of Archibald Hamilton, a Dublin solicitor, on Dominick Street Lower, among the law offices and lodging rooms north of the Liffey. Which day the birth belongs to is a question from the first hour: the third of August, or the fourth. He will settle it himself thirty years later, and not on astronomical grounds. The father's practice is unsteady and the household does not hold together. Before the boy is four he is sent out of it, to an uncle in another county. The house is 29 Dominick Street Lower, renumbered 36 afterwards.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: 29 Dominick Street Lower, Dublin, renumbered 36, the birthplace

stops.name: Talbot's Castle, Trim: the uncle's grammar
stops.date_confidence: About age three, so 1808 or 1809; month and day are unrecorded and defaulted to 01. The pin corrects the pool coordinate, which fell some 450 metres west into the town: Talbot's Castle stands inside the St Mary's Abbey precinct at 53.55528, -6.78694.
stops.campa: The Rev. James Hamilton keeps a school in a fifteenth-century abbey building on the Boyne, and into it comes a nephew of three who can already read English. The uncle teaches by immersion and by volume: Latin, Greek and Hebrew before the boy is five, then Persian, Arabic, Sanskrit, Syriac, and whatever else the shelves will support. Trim is a small town with a ruined Norman castle across the water. The parents stay in Dublin. For the next fifteen years this schoolroom is the whole of his home.
sources: Wikipedia, 'William Rowan Hamilton', drawing on R. P. Graves, Life of Sir William Rowan Hamilton
suggested_refs: Talbot's Castle in the St Mary's Abbey precinct, Trim, County Meath, the Rev. James Hamilton's school

stops.name: Dublin: against Zerah Colburn
stops.date_confidence: The sources disagree and the disagreement is left standing. The Colburn article dates the contest to September 1813, with Hamilton at eight, which fits his birth year; the Hamilton dossier put it around 1818. The venue of the exhibition is not identified in anything reached, and the pin is a generic Dublin city-centre point.
stops.campa: An American boy is being shown in Dublin for money. Zerah Colburn multiplies four-figure numbers in his head faster than the men in the room can write them down, and someone sets the Hamilton child against him. Hamilton loses. He is eight, and what he wants afterwards is not to be quicker but to know how it is done; from that question his arithmetic stops being a party trick and becomes a subject with rules under it. He goes back to Trim and the languages. Colburn goes on with the tour.
suggested_refs: Zerah Colburn's own Memoir (1833), on the Dublin exhibitions

stops.name: Trim: the Principia at sixteen
stops.date_confidence: Attested only as 'by around age sixteen', so the year is approximate; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: By sixteen he has worked through much of Newton's Principia, with analytic geometry and the differential calculus alongside it. Nobody in Trim set him this. The uncle's curriculum is languages and the classics, and the mathematics is what the boy does with the hours the curriculum leaves over. He reads Newton the way he read Persian, straight through and for possession. Having finished, he wants the continental writers next, which in the Ireland of 1821 means Laplace.
suggested_refs: Newton, Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, the book read at Trim

stops.name: Dublin: the flaw in Laplace
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day unrecorded and defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He takes up the Mecanique celeste and reads it as a text with a mistake in it. Laplace's demonstration of the parallelogram of forces will not do, and the seventeen-year-old writes out why. It is the most formidable mathematical book of the age and he is a schoolboy in County Meath with no teacher in the subject, no colleague in it, and no correspondent who could tell him whether he is right. This is the first thing he does that is not learning. The following July he sits the entrance examination at Trinity.
suggested_refs: Laplace, Mecanique celeste, and Hamilton's objection to the demonstration of the parallelogram of forces

stops.name: Dublin: Brinkley reads the papers
stops.date_confidence: December 1822 for the three papers reaching Brinkley. The remark quoted in the campa is dated 'about 1828' by the obituary that prints it and about 1822 by MacTutor; the contradiction is left open. A search of the full text of both volumes of Graves's Life returns no hit for the phrase, so Graves is not its source, and the obituarist disowns the wording in the next breath.
stops.campa: Three original papers are finished and passed to John Brinkley, Royal Astronomer of Ireland and Andrews Professor of Astronomy, who is about the only man in the country competent to read them. What Brinkley said afterwards gets quoted everywhere: that this young man, he did not say would be but was, the first mathematician of his age. The words reach print in an anonymous obituary of 1866 whose writer, in the very next sentence, says he knew Brinkley well and will undertake that he never went further than 'if the young man goes on as he has begun.'
sources: Unsigned obituary of Hamilton, conventionally attributed to Augustus De Morgan, The Gentleman's Magazine, New Series vol. 1 (January 1866), p. 129
MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: The Gentleman's Magazine obituary of January 1866, both for the Brinkley remark and for its immediate retraction

stops.name: Trinity College Dublin: the entrance examination
stops.date_confidence: July 1823 attested. The pin is the corrected Trinity coordinate, 53.3444, -6.2577, rather than the 53.3438, -6.2546 carried in older files, which sits about 215 metres from Front Square.
stops.campa: He enters in July 1823, at seventeen, after an examination the college goes on talking about, and comes first in classics and first in science. Twice the examiners award him an optime, a judgment they hand down perhaps once in a generation. The optics begins in his first year, and so does the classical reading, and he never afterwards sets either of them down. Undergraduates are not ordinarily read in the Transactions of the Royal Irish Academy; this one is submitting to them before he has a degree.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
oscar_wilde.journey.json, for the corrected Trinity College Dublin coordinate
suggested_refs: Trinity College Dublin entrance and examination records for 1823

stops.name: Edgeworthstown: Maria Edgeworth
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day unrecorded and defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: At the Edgeworth house in County Longford he is introduced to the novelist, then in her fifties and the best-known writer in Ireland. The correspondence begun here runs for the rest of her life and is not about mathematics. It is about books, people, and the running commentary of a woman who knows everybody worth knowing between Dublin and London. Hamilton writes verse and wants to be told it is good. Edgeworth tells him what she thinks, which is not always that, and keeps writing to him.
suggested_refs: The Hamilton and Edgeworth correspondence, printed in Graves, Life of Sir William Rowan Hamilton

stops.name: Summerhill, County Meath: Catherine Disney
stops.date_confidence: August 1824 for the introduction. The pool called Summerhill House the Disney family seat; Wikipedia's Summerhill article records the great house as the Langford and Rowley seat with no Disney connection, so that attribution is downgraded to reconstruction while the meeting at Summerhill stands. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 53.4895, -6.7368 to 53.481907, -6.73084.
stops.campa: His uncle takes him visiting, and at Summerhill he meets Catherine Disney. He is nineteen, an undergraduate with no income and no prospect of one for years; her family has other plans and does not entertain his. He writes a long poem called The Enthusiast about a grief he declines to name outright, and for twenty-eight years afterwards the subject keeps coming back in his letters, in his verse, and in what his friends say about his drinking. In 1825 she marries the Rev. William Barlow, a man some fifteen years her senior.
suggested_refs: Hamilton's poem The Enthusiast (1826)

stops.name: Royal Irish Academy, Grafton Street: On Caustics
stops.date_confidence: Communicated through Brinkley before the end of 1824 per MacTutor; the date of the reading is not given and December is an ordering device. The Academy occupied Navigation House at 114 Grafton Street until 1852, which is the pin used for all pre-1852 Academy stops in this file.
stops.campa: Brinkley communicates the undergraduate's first paper to the Academy: On Caustics, the geometry of the bright curve a family of light rays folds itself onto. The Academy's committee finds it too condensed to print and sends it back to be expanded. He expands it for three years. What comes back is a general method for handling any optical system whatever through one function, and it has a new title, the Theory of Systems of Rays. The Academy prints it.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: Hamilton, 'On Caustics', communicated to the Royal Irish Academy 1824

stops.name: Royal Irish Academy, Grafton Street: the Theory of Systems of Rays
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 23 April 1827, in MacTutor and in the Trinity College Dublin Hamilton archive.
stops.campa: He reads the mature first part of the Theory of Systems of Rays, and with it the characteristic function: one quantity, from which the entire behaviour of a system of rays can be recovered by differentiation. Reflection, refraction, focus and aberration all drop out of a single expression. He is twenty-one and has not taken his degree. Within seven years he does the same thing to mechanics, replacing the tracking of forces on bodies with the differentiation of one function.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: Hamilton, 'Theory of Systems of Rays', Transactions of the Royal Irish Academy vol. 15 (1828)

stops.name: Dunsink Observatory: Royal Astronomer of Ireland
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (1827). The month is set to follow Brinkley's elevation to the see of Cloyne and to order this stop after the April reading; it is not itself attested in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: Brinkley is made Bishop of Cloyne and the two offices he held fall vacant together: the Andrews Professorship of Astronomy and the post of Royal Astronomer of Ireland. Trinity elects an undergraduate to both. Hamilton is twenty-one, has never sat for a fellowship, and is not much of a practical observer. The Board knows all of this and elects him on the strength of the optics. He moves into the observatory house on the hill at Dunsink, five miles out from the college, and lives there for thirty-eight years.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: Dunsink Observatory, County Dublin, residence and post from 1827 to 1865

stops.name: Rydal Mount: Wordsworth reads the poems
stops.date_confidence: September 1827, during an English and Scottish tour made just after the Dunsink appointment; the day is not given. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 54.443, -2.9787, which falls some 680 metres off the property, to 54.4487, -2.9824.
stops.campa: Newly appointed and touring England, he walks up to Rydal Mount carrying a sheaf of his own verse. Wordsworth receives him and reads the poems, then tells him plainly that his gift is mathematics and not poetry. Hamilton accepts the verdict and disregards it, and goes on writing verse and sending it to poets for the rest of his life. That night the two of them walk the road between their lodgings back and forth in the dark, neither willing to let the conversation end.
suggested_refs: The Hamilton and Wordsworth correspondence in Graves, Life of Sir William Rowan Hamilton

stops.name: Curraghchase, County Limerick: Ellen de Vere refuses him
stops.date_confidence: The proposal and the refusal in 1831 are in the biographies and were not independently confirmed in this pass; the placing at Curraghchase is reconstruction. Wikipedia's Curraghchase article documents the de Vere family there but mentions neither Ellen de Vere nor the proposal. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 52.6335, -8.8467 to 52.59444, -8.87083. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Six years after Catherine Disney's marriage he asks Ellen de Vere to marry him, and is refused. The de Veres of Curraghchase stay his friends and correspondents; it is a house of poets, and Aubrey de Vere the younger will be one of them. Hamilton is twice refused now, twenty-six years old, Royal Astronomer of Ireland, and living in an observatory five miles outside the city with nobody in it but the staff. Within two years he is married to somebody else. The refusal is on the record; her reasons for it are not.
suggested_refs: Graves, Life of Sir William Rowan Hamilton, vol. 1, on the de Vere connection

stops.name: Highgate: Coleridge at The Grove
stops.date_confidence: Year carried from the pool, which took the visit from the dossier rather than from a fetched primary letter; month and day defaulted to 01. Independent confirmation from Graves or the Highgate circle's correspondence was not obtained in this pass.
stops.campa: In the house on The Grove where Coleridge has lived a decade under his physician's roof, the Royal Astronomer of Ireland comes to talk metaphysics with a poet who has read his Kant. Hamilton leaves with a possibility hardened into a programme, and the paper he publishes five years later, on algebra as the science of pure time, is an argument of that kind carried out in equations. What the two of them go at in the room is the philosophy of science, the trinity, and whether algebra rests on something prior to number.
suggested_refs: The Grove, Highgate, the house of James Gillman where Coleridge lodged from 1823

stops.name: Nenagh, County Tipperary: marriage to Helen Maria Bayly
stops.date_confidence: The year 1833 is attested; the day, 9 April, is carried from the pool as reconstruction and was not confirmed against a marriage register in this pass. The pin is the town where her father, the Rev. Henry Bayly, was rector.
stops.campa: He marries Helen Maria Bayly, daughter of the rector of Nenagh, a retiring and frequently unwell woman he has known a short time. She will be away from Dunsink for long stretches, staying with her own people for months at a time and once for the better part of a year, while the observatory runs without a mistress in it. Three children come of the marriage. Every visitor to the house over the next thirty years remarks on the disorder of the place, the papers on every surface, and the master of it working through the night in rooms nobody has tidied.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: The Bayly rectory at Nenagh, County Tipperary

stops.name: Bayly Farm, near Dunsink: the honeymoon
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor names the honeymoon site only as Bayly Farm, across the fields from the observatory; no more precise address was found, and the coordinate is an approximation near Dunsink rather than a located landmark. The month orders the stop after the marriage and is not attested.
stops.campa: The wedding journey goes as far as a farm belonging to his wife's relations, across the fields from the observatory he already lives in. Through these weeks he is at work on the third supplement to the Theory of Systems of Rays, the one that will carry the prediction of conical refraction, and what the family remembers of the honeymoon afterwards is chiefly the writing. Helen will spend a good part of the next decade back at this farm with the children. From the yard she can see the dome of the house she has married into.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: Hamilton, Third Supplement to an Essay on the Theory of Systems of Rays, in progress at the farm

stops.name: Royal Irish Academy, Grafton Street: a prediction out of the wave surface
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 22 October 1832, from the Trinity College Dublin Hamilton archive page on conical refraction.
stops.campa: Working on Fresnel's wave surface for biaxial crystals, he finds singular points the geometry demands and no experimenter has ever reported. A single ray entering such a crystal along the right axis should emerge not as a ray but as a hollow cone of light, and at the surface as a cone again. Nothing in optics has been arrived at this way before, out of a function, ahead of any observation, and the claim is either a theorem or an embarrassment. He reads it to the Academy on the twenty-second of October 1832.
sources: Trinity College Dublin, David R. Wilkins Hamilton archive, 'Conical Refraction'
maths.tcd.ie, Humphrey Lloyd, report on conical refraction to the British Association
suggested_refs: Hamilton, Third Supplement to the Theory of Systems of Rays, read 22 October 1832

stops.name: Trinity College Dublin: Lloyd's aragonite
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 14 December 1832, for the observation of external conical refraction. Lloyd's confirmation of the internal cone followed, and he reported the work to the British Association at Cambridge in 1833; that Cambridge appearance is Lloyd's own journey and is cited here rather than staged as a scene in Hamilton's file.
stops.campa: Hamilton cannot do the experiment. He asks Humphrey Lloyd, the college's experimental physicist, who can. Lloyd needs a crystal both large and clear, settles on aragonite, and fails for weeks until the aperture is small enough. Two months after the prediction was read out, in a room a few hundred yards from the hall where it was read, on the fourteenth of December, he sees it: a ring of light where a spot ought to be, the cone the equations ordered.
sources: Trinity College Dublin, David R. Wilkins Hamilton archive, 'Conical Refraction'
Humphrey Lloyd, report of the experiments, maths.tcd.ie
suggested_refs: Humphrey Lloyd's 1833 report to the British Association at Cambridge on internal conical refraction

stops.name: Dunsink Observatory: a general method in dynamics
stops.date_confidence: The first essay appeared in the Philosophical Transactions in 1834 and the second in 1835. The pin is Dunsink, where they were written, not London, where they were printed; Hamilton did not travel for either. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He turns the optical method on mechanics. If a system of rays can be handed over to one characteristic function, so can a system of moving bodies: planetary orbits, the swing of a pendulum, the whole of motion becoming derivatives of a single quantity. The Philosophical Transactions print it in two essays, in 1834 and 1835. Jacobi at Konigsberg takes the method up and completes it, and the equations go under both names. Hamilton is finished with dynamics inside three years and back at algebra.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: Hamilton, 'On a General Method in Dynamics', Philosophical Transactions (1834), and the Second Essay (1835)

stops.name: Dublin: the medals and the sword
stops.date_confidence: The Cunningham Medal is dated 1834, the Royal Medal and the knighthood 1835; months and days are not given in the sources consulted and are defaulted to 01. The pool called the 1834 Cunningham Medal the Academy's first: it was not, the medal having been awarded since 1796. This was Hamilton's first of two, the second coming in 1848.
stops.campa: The Royal Irish Academy gives him the Cunningham Medal for conical refraction in 1834, the Royal Society a Royal Medal the year after. In 1835 the British Association meets in Dublin with Hamilton serving as secretary, and the Lord Lieutenant knights him there, at thirty. He is the most decorated man in Irish science, married eighteen months, one son in the house and another coming. He has told nobody that he has been stuck for a decade on a problem he cannot state to anyone: how to multiply triplets.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: Royal Irish Academy records of the Cunningham Medal, 1834 and 1848

stops.name: Bristol: the British Association, and an empty house at home
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor places Hamilton at a Bristol meeting of the British Association in the autumn following 1835; the Association's sixth meeting was at Bristol in 1836, which pins the year and lifts the pool's hedge. The venue within Bristol is not identified, and month and day are defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He crosses to England for the Association's sixth meeting, at Bristol in the autumn. Helen has taken the children to her family's farm and remains there ten months. The Dunsink household in these years runs on his sisters, his students and a table of correspondence nobody opens. He is thirty-one, holds already every honour the two islands have to give, and works at night on a question no colleague has asked him to solve and no journal is waiting on. The quaternions are seven years off.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
Wikipedia, list of British Science Association annual meetings
suggested_refs: Report of the Sixth Meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science, Bristol 1836

segments.name: Algebra as the Science of Pure Time

stops.name: Royal Irish Academy, Grafton Street: the algebra of couples
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 4 November 1833, per MacTutor.
stops.campa: He reads a paper defining a complex number as an ordered pair of reals, with rules for adding and multiplying pairs, and no square root of minus one anywhere in the definition. The imaginary quantity that mathematicians had used for two centuries while apologising for it stops being a mystery and becomes two ordinary numbers with a multiplication table. Having built the plane out of pairs, he asks the next question. It takes him ten years to answer: what is space built out of?
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: Hamilton, 'Theory of Conjugate Functions, or Algebraic Couples', read 4 November 1833

stops.name: Dunsink Observatory: three children and a moved birthday
stops.date_confidence: William Edwin born 10 May 1834, Archibald Henry on 4 August 1835, Helen Eliza Amelia in 1840; the stop is dated to the middle birth. Hamilton's own birth fell at midnight between the third and fourth of August 1805, and Wikipedia records that he fixed on the fourth after this son was born on that day.
stops.campa: William Edwin comes in 1834, Archibald Henry on the fourth of August 1835, Helen Eliza Amelia in 1840. Archibald will become a clergyman, and the man to whom his father writes the last full account of the quaternions. The second birth settles a question thirty years old: Hamilton had been born at midnight, on the boundary between the third of August and the fourth, and had never been made to choose. Now the boy's birthday falls on the fourth, and the father takes the fourth for his own.
suggested_refs: The Broome Bridge letter of 5 August 1865 to the Rev. Archibald Henry Hamilton

stops.name: Dunsink Observatory: algebra as the science of pure time
stops.date_confidence: The essay appeared in Transactions of the Royal Irish Academy vol. 17 (1837), its parts read from 1833 onward; month and day defaulted to 01. Both quoted passages were read directly from the D. R. Wilkins edition of the 1837 text, the opening at p. 293 and the passage below in Article II.
stops.campa: The couples paper comes out with a long essay of philosophy in front of it. Geometry, he argues, is the science of space; there must be a science standing to time as geometry stands to space, and that science is algebra. Number is neither counting nor measuring, it is pure succession, and the whole of algebra follows from the intuition of order in time. Continental mathematicians receive this as ballast they did not order. The essay opens by dividing algebra into three schools, the Practical, the Philological and the Theoretical, and declares for the third.
stops.quote: The notion or intuition of Order in Time is not less but more deep-seated in the human mind, than the notion of intuition of Order in Space; and a mathematical Science may be founded on the former, as pure and as demonstrative as the science founded on the latter
stops.quote_source: Hamilton, 'Theory of Conjugate Functions, or Algebraic Couples; with a Preliminary and Elementary Essay on Algebra as the Science of Pure Time', Transactions of the Royal Irish Academy vol. 17 (1837), Article II, in the edition of D. R. Wilkins, Trinity College Dublin
sources: Hamilton, Transactions of the Royal Irish Academy vol. 17 (1837), Wilkins edition PDF
MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: The General Introductory Remarks to the 1837 essay, p. 293, on the three schools of algebra

stops.name: Royal Irish Academy, Grafton Street: the president's chair
stops.date_confidence: Year attested for both the election and the Trinity M.A.; the month is an ordering device to keep this stop after the essay and is not attested. He held the presidency until 1846.
stops.campa: At thirty-one he is elected President of the Royal Irish Academy, and takes his M.A. from Trinity in the same year, ten years after being handed a professorial chair without a degree. The Academy is a body of antiquarians, physicians and landed gentlemen with a scattering of working scientists among them, and its president is expected to preside, to correspond and to keep the peace. He does all three. He holds the chair for nine years and resigns it in 1846.
suggested_refs: Royal Irish Academy presidential records, 1837 to 1846

stops.name: The Royal Canal towpath, Cabra: the walk into town
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 16 October 1843, in Hamilton's own letters of 15 October 1858 to Tait and 5 August 1865 to his son.
stops.campa: He is walking into town along the canal with his wife, on his way to preside at a Council meeting of the Academy, and the thing that has defeated him for fifteen years gives way on the towpath. Triplets will not multiply. Quadruples will, if he gives up the rule that the order of the factors makes no difference. Helen is talking beside him. He has three imaginary units where there was one, each squaring to minus one, and the product of any two of them is the third, with a sign that depends on which came first.
stops.quote: An electric circuit seemed to close; and a spark flashed forth, the herald (as I foresaw, immediately) of many long years to come of definitely directed thought and work
stops.quote_source: Hamilton to his son the Rev. Archibald Henry Hamilton, 5 August 1865, in R. P. Graves, Life of Sir William Rowan Hamilton, vol. 2, ch. XXVIII, as reproduced by the School of Mathematics, Trinity College Dublin
sources: Trinity College Dublin, Hamilton letters archive, the Broome Bridge letter
suggested_refs: The Royal Canal towpath from Cabra to the city, the route of the walk

stops.name: Brougham Bridge, Cabra: cut with a knife on a stone
stops.date_confidence: Attested, the same day, in the 1865 letter to Archibald. No trace of the original carving survives; the equation visible near the bridge today is a later hand. The exponents in the quotation are rendered in the source page as 'i2' for i squared.
stops.campa: They come up to Brougham Bridge, where the road into town crosses the canal, and he takes out a penknife. Fifteen years of work, four symbols and a minus sign, scratched into a parapet on the way to a committee meeting. He calls the impulse unphilosophical in the only first-hand account of it that exists, written twenty-two years afterwards, a month before his death. What he cuts into the stone is i squared, j squared, k squared and ijk, each of them equal to minus one.
stops.quote: Nor could I resist the impulse - unphilosophical as it may have been - to cut with a knife on a stone of Brougham Bridge, as we passed it, the fundamental formula with the symbols, i, j, k; namely, i2 = j2 = k2 = ijk = -1
stops.quote_source: Hamilton to his son the Rev. Archibald Henry Hamilton, 5 August 1865, in Graves, Life of Sir William Rowan Hamilton, vol. 2, ch. XXVIII, text of the School of Mathematics, Trinity College Dublin
sources: Trinity College Dublin, Hamilton letters archive, the Broome Bridge letter
suggested_refs: Brougham Bridge, now Broom Bridge, over the Royal Canal at Cabra

stops.name: Royal Irish Academy, Grafton Street: the announcement
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 13 November 1843, in the Trinity College Dublin archive materials and corroborated in MacTutor and Wikipedia.
stops.campa: Four weeks after the towpath he reads the paper. A quaternion: a number with four parts, one real and three imaginary, obeying every rule of arithmetic but one. Multiplication here is not commutative, ij is not ji, and no mathematician in 1843 has a precedent for an algebra that breaks that rule and goes on working. Everything he does for the remaining twenty-two years comes out of this paper. He had asked leave to read it before the Council meeting of the sixteenth of October was over.
stops.quote: Less than an hour elapsed before I had asked and obtained leave of the Council of the Royal Irish Academy...to read at the next General Meeting a Paper on Quaternions
stops.quote_source: Hamilton to Peter Guthrie Tait, 15 October 1858, in Graves, Life of Sir William Rowan Hamilton, vol. 2, as reproduced by the School of Mathematics, Trinity College Dublin
sources: Trinity College Dublin, Hamilton letters archive
MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: Hamilton's quaternion paper read to the Royal Irish Academy, 13 November 1843

stops.name: Dublin: the Geological Society dinner
stops.date_confidence: February 1846 per MacTutor, which carries the phrase quoted in the campa. The specific venue of the Geological Society of Dublin's meeting was not identified in anything reached, so the pin is a generic city-centre point and the day is defaulted.
stops.campa: At a meeting of the Geological Society of Dublin he makes an exhibition of himself through his intoxication, and that wording is the record's own. It happens in the city where he is President of the Royal Irish Academy and the best-known man of science in the country, and it is not forgotten. From here his drinking is discussed in his friends' letters in the tone people keep for an illness, and in the biographies in the tone they keep for a moral. He resigns the presidency the same year.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: Graves, Life of Sir William Rowan Hamilton, vol. 2, on the years after 1846

stops.name: Trinity College Dublin: lecturing on quaternions
stops.date_confidence: June 1848 for the lecture course, attested from the other side of the encounter in arthur_cayley.journey.json and in Wikipedia's Hamilton article. The pin here is Cayley's existing Trinity coordinate, kept byte-identical so the two files meet at one point on the map; Hamilton's other Trinity stops in this file carry the corrected 53.3444, -6.2577.
stops.campa: He begins lecturing on quaternions in the halls of Trinity, and among the men who cross over to hear him is Arthur Cayley, twenty-seven, a conveyancing pupil in London chambers doing mathematics in the hours the law leaves free. Cayley likes him and keeps up with him for the rest of Hamilton's life. The metaphysics he never takes: from a president's chair at Southport, thirty-five years later, he says he cannot himself recognise the connection of algebra with the notion of time.
sources: arthur_cayley.journey.json, stop 'Trinity College Dublin: Hamilton on quaternions'
Alexander Macfarlane, Lectures on Ten British Mathematicians of the Nineteenth Century (1916), ch. 5
suggested_refs: Cayley's presidential address to the British Association, Southport, 1883, on algebra and the notion of time

stops.name: Dunsink Observatory: Lectures on Quaternions
stops.date_confidence: Year attested for publication by Hodges and Smith of Dublin; month and day defaulted to 01. The pin is where the book was written rather than the publisher's premises.
stops.campa: Lectures on Quaternions is published in Dublin by Hodges and Smith: a systematic statement of the new method, and by common consent an unusable introduction to it. The method is powerful and the exposition is impenetrable. The book records the history of its author's thinking instead of teaching the reader the calculus, and its replacement will still be half-written when he dies twelve years later. He knows this much already, and begins at once on a shorter and plainer book.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: Hamilton, Lectures on Quaternions (Dublin: Hodges and Smith, 1853)

stops.name: Dunsink Observatory: the pencil case from Catherine
stops.date_confidence: 1853, in the last months of Catherine Disney Barlow's life; MacTutor carries the pencil case, the inscription, the visit and her death two weeks afterwards. The pool's 'November' for the death was not confirmed and is dropped. The month here is an ordering device. Where the deathbed visit took place is nowhere recorded in the sources consulted, so the pin is Hamilton's own house and not the site of the meeting.
stops.campa: Twenty-eight years after her marriage, dying, Catherine Disney Barlow sends him a pencil case with an inscription cut into it. He goes to her. He carries a copy of Lectures on Quaternions, the work of his life, and puts it into her hands. For the twelve years left to him he tells the story to nearly everyone he corresponds with, at length and repeatedly, in letters that otherwise concern the algebra of space and the multiplication of four-part numbers. She dies two weeks after the visit.
stops.quote: From one who you must never forget, nor think unkindly of, and who would have died more contented if we had once more met.
stops.quote_source: Inscription on the pencil case sent by Catherine Disney Barlow to Hamilton in 1853, quoted in the MacTutor History of Mathematics biography of Hamilton
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: Graves, Life of Sir William Rowan Hamilton, vol. 2, on the Disney correspondence

stops.name: Dublin: the Icosian Game
stops.date_confidence: The icosian calculus dates from 1856 and was presented with the game at the twenty-seventh meeting of the British Association, Dublin, in August 1857. The sale of the rights is dated 1857 by Wikipedia and by puzzlemuseum, with marketing from 1859; the pool's single date of 1859 for the sale is corrected here and the discrepancy is left visible rather than smoothed.
stops.campa: Out of the quaternions he makes a smaller algebra, the icosian calculus, whose symbols track movement along the edges of a dodecahedron; and out of the calculus he makes a puzzle. Find a route through all twenty vertices touching each once and returning to the start. He shows it at the British Association in Dublin. On John T. Graves's advice he sells the rights to Jaques of London for twenty-five pounds, and the firm issues it as The Icosian Game and as The Travellers Dodecahedron, or a voyage round the world. A handful of original sets survive.
sources: Trinity College Dublin, David R. Wilkins Hamilton archive, 'Icosian Calculus'
suggested_refs: The Icosian Game and The Travellers Dodecahedron, Jaques of London, issued 1859; surviving examples in the Hordern-Dalgety Collection

stops.name: Dunsink Observatory: the letters to Tait
stops.date_confidence: The correspondence with Peter Guthrie Tait began in August 1858, per MacTutor's Tait biography, which quotes Tait's letter of 7 December 1858. The pool's claim that the two men met in 1858 is not supported: no meeting in person is documented in the sources consulted, and the entry is reworded here as a correspondence. The stop is dated to Hamilton's own letter of 15 October 1858.
stops.campa: A young professor at Edinburgh writes to him about a formula he had admired years earlier on page 610 of the Lectures and then left alone. Tait has come back to quaternions by way of Helmholtz on the motion of fluids, and he will spend the next thirty years arguing for them in print more effectively than their inventor ever manages. Hamilton answers at length, and in one of these letters sets down the fullest account he will ever write of what happened on the towpath fifteen years before. Nothing in the record puts the two men in a room together.
stops.quote: I felt a problem to have been at that moment solved, an intellectual want relieved, which had haunted me for at least fifteen years before
stops.quote_source: Hamilton to Peter Guthrie Tait, 15 October 1858, in Graves, Life of Sir William Rowan Hamilton, vol. 2, as reproduced by the School of Mathematics, Trinity College Dublin
sources: Trinity College Dublin, Hamilton letters archive
MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Peter Guthrie Tait

stops.name: Dunsink Observatory: the Elements outgrows its plan
stops.date_confidence: The last six years at Dunsink went to the Elements of Quaternions; 1860 is an ordering date for a period, not an event. The bronchial or respiratory illness carried in the pool for these years is in neither Wikipedia nor MacTutor nor the Trinity College page, and is not repeated here.
stops.campa: The short plain book turns into the Elements of Quaternions and does not stop growing. He is not observing much and the Board has stopped expecting it; one book comes out of the house at Dunsink now, and it is not finished. He works at it through attacks of gout, through days when he does not leave the house, and through a correspondence he long ago stopped keeping up with, in rooms that fill with unanswered letters and with plates of food set down on top of the manuscript.
stops.quote: Hamilton was apt to work by fits and starts
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Augustus De Morgan, 'Sir W. R. Hamilton', The Gentleman's Magazine (January 1866), seen through a secondary aggregator and not confirmed against the original text in this pass
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'

stops.name: Dunsink Observatory: elected in Washington
stops.date_confidence: Year attested for the election, which was made in absentia; month and day defaulted to 01. The pin is Hamilton's own house, not the Academy in Washington, which he never saw.
stops.campa: The United States, in the middle of its civil war, founds a National Academy of Sciences, and the first list of foreign associates carries his name. He is fifty-eight, has never crossed the Atlantic, and does not travel to be admitted. Ireland knighted him thirty years ago, and this is the last honour that will reach him. The notice comes to the observatory, where the manuscript of the Elements is stacked in every room and he is at work on a chapter he will not finish.

stops.name: Dunsink Observatory: the letter to Archibald
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 5 August 1865, from the text held by the Trinity College Dublin Hamilton archive; four weeks before his death.
stops.campa: His son asks him how the quaternions came, and he sits down and writes the whole thing out: the walk along the canal with the boy's mother, the closing of the circuit, the spark, the knife, the stone of the bridge. He is careful about the date, and careful to mark off which parts he remembers from which he is reconstructing at twenty-two years' distance. He writes it in a house where the unfinished book is stacked on the floor, four weeks before he dies. Every account of that morning that anybody has ever written descends from this letter. It is dated the fifth of August 1865.
sources: Trinity College Dublin, David R. Wilkins Hamilton archive, the Broome Bridge letter of 5 August 1865
suggested_refs: Graves, Life of Sir William Rowan Hamilton, vol. 2, ch. XXVIII, where the letter is printed

stops.name: Dunsink Observatory: death
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 2 September 1865, aged sixty. Both Wikipedia and MacTutor give the cause as a severe attack of gout; the respiratory illness in the pool's chronology is not in those sources and is dropped.
stops.campa: He dies at the observatory on the second of September, after a severe attack of gout, at sixty. He had lived in this house for thirty-eight years, since being elected to it as an undergraduate who had not yet sat his degree examinations, and never held another post anywhere, nor applied for one. The Elements of Quaternions lies on the table unfinished, its last chapter incomplete and its plan long past anyone's control. His eldest son will have to close it and see it through the press.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
suggested_refs: Dunsink Observatory, the house where he died

Helen follows him into the ground in 1869, and other family after her. The cemetery keeps his name on the list it prints of its notable dead, and the entry runs to a line. Past the bare fact of the interment the record goes quiet. Which plot, what the stone says, whether it still stands: the biographical dictionary returns a redirect error and the grave registry returns a refusal.

stops.name: Dunsink Observatory: the vectors take the field
stops.date_confidence: This stop compresses reception rather than an event. The displacement of quaternions by the vector analysis of Gibbs and Heaviside runs from about the 1880s; the date is an ordering device and the pin is Hamilton's own observatory, not a place any of the disputants stood. The quotation is Kelvin's, written in December 1892, twenty-seven years after Hamilton's death.
stops.campa: Within twenty years of his death the instrument he built for physics is taken apart and the useful half kept. Gibbs at Yale and Heaviside in England pull the vector out of the quaternion, drop the real part and the awkward product, and hand engineers a notation that does the same work with less apparatus. Tait fights for the whole system and loses. William Thomson, Lord Kelvin, writing privately in 1892 about somebody else's textbook, gives the judgment the next generation repeats.
stops.quote: Quaternions came from Hamilton after his really good work had been done ; and, though beautifully ingenious, have been an unmixed evil to those who have touched them in any way, including Clerk Maxwell.
stops.quote_source: William Thomson, Lord Kelvin, to R. B. Hayward, December 1892, printed in Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson, Baron Kelvin of Largs (Macmillan, 1910), vol. 2, ch. XXV, p. 1138
sources: Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910), vol. 2, p. 1138

stops.name: Broom Bridge, Cabra: the plaque
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 13 November 1958, for the unveiling, on the anniversary of the Academy paper rather than of the walk. The plaque was later moved higher on the structure and set back behind the railing, on a date not given in the sources. The pin is the afterlife coordinate for the bridge and differs slightly from the discovery-day pin earlier in this file.
stops.campa: Ninety-three years after his death a bronze plaque goes up under the bridge, unveiled on the anniversary of the Academy paper rather than of the walk. The stone he actually cut is not there: no trace of the 1843 carving survives, and what visitors find scratched near the plaque is other people's handwriting. The plaque itself wears down under the hands of the people who come to touch it, and is lifted higher on the structure and set back behind the railing, out of their reach. What date that was done on is not recorded either.
stops.quote: Here as he walked by on the 16th of October 1843 Sir William Rowan Hamilton in a flash of genius discovered the fundamental formula for quaternion multiplication i2 = j2 = k2 = ijk = -1 & cut it on a stone of this bridge.
stops.quote_source: Bronze plaque at Broom Bridge, Royal Canal, Dublin, unveiled by Taoiseach Eamon de Valera on 13 November 1958; text as given in Wikipedia, 'Broom Bridge'

stops.name: Dunsink Observatory: the walk on the sixteenth
stops.date_confidence: The walk has been made annually on 16 October since 1989, and the date here is the first of them. The names listed are recorded in the Broom Bridge article as people who have joined over the years; they are given as a list of record and no one of them is staged as a scene in Hamilton's file.
stops.campa: Since 1989 mathematicians have walked the route on the sixteenth of October: out of the observatory gate, down through the fields and along the canal to the bridge, the ground he covered on foot with his wife on the way to a committee meeting. Dublin calls the day Broomsday, after the other walk the city keeps. Among those who have made it are the physicists Murray Gell-Mann, Steven Weinberg and Frank Wilczek, and the mathematicians Andrew Wiles, Roger Penrose and Ingrid Daubechies.

stops.name: Trinity College Dublin: the bicentenary
stops.date_confidence: Year attested for the Hamilton Mathematics Institute and for the Central Bank of Ireland's silver proof coin; the two commemorative stamps are dated 13 November 1943. The pin is the Trinity coordinate carried by the pool for the Institute. Month and day defaulted to 01. The closing sentence reaches past Hamilton's own life into present-day computing and is flagged as such in the report.
stops.campa: Ireland put him on two stamps in 1943 for the centenary of the quaternions and struck a ten-euro coin for the bicentenary of his birth. Trinity founds a Hamilton Mathematics Institute in 2005 and puts his name on a building; Maynooth names an institute after him too; there is a crater on the Moon. The algebra itself comes back in the same decades, not in physics but in the arithmetic of rotation, where four numbers turn without locking: graphics engines, robot arms and spacecraft turning in the dark all compute their attitude in quaternions.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
